name: Hair spray

card.summary: An aerosol or pump spray that coats hair in a thin polymer film to hold a style in place and keep volume and shape through the day.
card.note: Inhalation of overspray is the main safety concern; use in ventilated spaces per product labels.

quick.overview:
Hair spray is a styling product that deposits film-forming polymers on the hair as its solvent evaporates, fixing a style in place. It is weaker than gel or wax and is often used as a finishing step [1][2].

For appearance it keeps volume, hairlines and flyaways where they were styled, and holds a look through wind and humidity. Hold ranges from flexible to maximum, depending on the polymer blend [1].
quick.how: It is sprayed over dry or finished styling from a distance, either to set the whole look or to tame particular areas, and brushed out afterwards to avoid a stiff, crunchy feel [2]. People pair it with blow-drying, texturising products or volumisers, and the effect lasts until the hair is washed.
quick.risks: Styling products can dry hair, and buildup may cause dullness, breakage or scalp irritation [2]. Inhaling overspray is the main concern: studies have examined acute airway responses to hair-spray preparations, and rare case reports describe lung or heart problems [3][4][5]. Aerosol propellants were changed from CFCs to hydrocarbons and other gases because of ozone concerns [1][2].

lead: Hair spray, also called hair lacquer or spritz, is a styling product sprayed onto hair to resist humidity and wind and keep a shape in place for hours [1]. Its active ingredients are film-forming polymers dissolved in solvents, delivered by aerosol can or pump [1][2]. Most of what is in the can is solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, with a smaller share of polymers such as polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) and polyvinyl acetate copolymers that provide the hold [1].

For appearance, the benefit is shape retention. As the solvent evaporates, the polymers leave a thin film that bonds strands in their styled position, keeping volume, height, parting, hairline styling and flyaways where they were put [1]. Products are sold in flexible, medium and maximum hold, and Wikipedia describes the effect as weaker than gel or wax, which is why hair spray is commonly used as a finishing layer over blow-dried, backcombed or sculpted styles [1][2].

Hair sprays were developed in Europe in the 1920s and spread in the United States with the aerosol can in the 1940s; Chase Products is credited with the first US packaging in 1948 [1]. By 1964 hair spray was the best-selling beauty product in the US, it declined in the 1970s, and it returned with the big hair of the 1980s [1]. Medical literature on hair spray concerns inhalation safety rather than styling performance, including a 1974 controlled trial of airway responses, a 1964 report on hair-spray thesaurosis and a 2022 cardiomyopathy case report [3][4][5].

paras: A hair spray has several functional parts: a polymer concentrate that forms the film, plasticizers that keep the film from becoming brittle, solvents that carry everything and evaporate, fragrance and luster agents, and a propellant in aerosol versions [1]. The concentrate is a small share of the can; most of the contents are solvents such as isopropanol and ethanol [1].

The polymer blend sets the character of the hold. PVP is noted for conferring stiffness, copolymers with vinyl acetate are common, and vinyl acetate-crotonic acid copolymers produce harder films, which lets manufacturers tune products to flexible, medium or maximum hold [1]. Plasticizers such as aminomethyl propanol, esters of citric and adipic acid, surfactants such as benzalkonium chloride, silicones such as dimethicone and polyglycols adjust adhesion, flexibility and feel [1]. Wikipedia's article on hairstyling products adds polydimethylsiloxane as a water-insoluble polymer used for longer hold, and maleic anhydride copolymers among the common polymers [2].

'Natural' hair sprays use plant gums such as gum arabic (from acacia sap) or gum tragacanth dissolved in alcohol instead of synthetic polymers [2]. Pump sprays deliver the same type of solution without a pressurised propellant [2].

Hair spray is applied over dry or finished styling, held at a distance, to set the whole look or tame particular areas such as a fringe, crown or flyaways [2]. Its stated purpose is to resist wind and humidity and keep a style's shape [1]. Because the film is weaker than that of gel or wax, spray is usually a final step rather than the main shaping product, and the stiff feel it can leave is commonly softened by brushing out [2].

Wikipedia's hairstyling-product article places spray alongside other options: gel stiffens hair more strongly and is most often used by men; wax holds hair while leaving it pliable; mousse is a foam applied to damp roots before blow-drying to add volume; pomade suits slick, tight styles and does not dry; and volumizers use humectants and polymers to add body to fine or flat hair [2]. Hair spray is used with these, for example over a blow-dried, mousse-built style to keep volume through the day [2].

Early hair sprays were developed in Europe in the 1920s [1]. In the United States they arrived alongside the aerosol can in the 1940s, and patents for hair-styling copolymers were issued in 1940 and 1945 [1]. In 1948 Chase Products, an aerosol manufacturer based in Broadview, Illinois, became the first in the US to package hair spray, after the beauty industry saw that wartime insecticide aerosol cans could dispense it [1][2].

Hair spray became the highest-selling beauty product in 1964, driven by updos and similar structured styles [1]. At the 1968 Miss America protest, feminist demonstrators placed hair spray among items they called 'instruments of female torture' in a 'Freedom Trash Can' [1]. Sales fell in the 1970s as straight, loose hairstyles dominated, and popularity returned in the 1980s with big hair associated with the glam metal scene [1].

Hair spray has also been used off the head, for instance on legs or inside a dress to keep fabric in place, and the extremophile bacterium Microbacterium hatanonis has been found living in hair spray [1].

Before 1979 chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were the most popular aerosol propellants, and they were replaced because of environmental concerns about ozone depletion [1][2]. After the phase-out in the 1980s, hydrocarbons such as propane, butane and isobutane became popular [1]. Because hydrocarbons are poor solvents for the polymers, dimethyl ether is often added as both propellant and solvent [1]. Fluorinated gases also replaced CFCs, most commonly 1,1-difluoroethane (HFC-152a) [1]. Pump sprays avoid propellants altogether [2].

Wikipedia notes that most styling products do not damage hair when used properly, but any product can dry hair out, some ingredients strip natural oils, and buildup can cause dullness, dryness, breakage, thinning or scalp irritation such as eczema [2].

Inhalation is the main safety subject in the medical literature. A 1974 controlled clinical trial in the New England Journal of Medicine examined acute airway responses to hair-spray preparations [3]. A 1964 report in Food and Cosmetics Toxicology described 'hair-spray thesaurosis', a term for lung changes attributed to inhaled hair-spray polymer [4]. A 2022 case report described hair-spray-induced cardiomyopathy [5]. These are individual reports and small studies; none quantifies risk for ordinary styling use.

Published human research on hair spray concerns safety rather than styling performance: a 1974 controlled clinical trial of acute airway responses [3], a 1964 report of hair-spray thesaurosis [4] and a 2022 case report on cardiomyopathy [5]. No trials of hold, durability or hair appearance were found.

timeline.event: First US patent for hair-styling copolymers issued, with another in 1945 [1].
Chase Products of Broadview, Illinois, first to package hair spray in the US [1][2].
Hair spray becomes the top-selling US beauty product [1].
Miss America protest places hair spray in a 'Freedom Trash Can' [1].
Controlled trial of acute airway responses to hair spray published [3].
CFC propellants, previously the most popular, begin to be replaced; phase-out continues through the 1980s [1].
Big-hair styles revive hair spray sales [1].
